title: A Good Name, a Child's Way, and the Words of the Wise
summary: The first sixteen verses close the long collection of Solomon's proverbs with sayings on a good name, the rich and poor who share one Maker, training a child, debt, generosity, and the oppression of the poor. At verse 17 a new voice begins: the words of the wise, a collection of longer sayings introduced with a call to listen and a promise of thirty sayings, which warns against robbing the poor, befriending the hot-tempered, pledging for debts, and moving ancient boundary stones.
story: This chapter marks a seam in the book. The collection headed The proverbs of Solomon at 10:1 ends at 22:16, after exactly 375 verses. Verse 17 opens a new section, often called the Words of the Wise, which runs to 24:22 and is followed by a short appendix (24:23-34). The form changes noticeably: instead of self-contained two-line sayings, the new section uses longer units of two or more verses, often with commands and reasons, and the teacher addresses the reader directly as you, much like the father of chapters 1 to 9. The book is gathering wisdom from more than one source, all placed under the fear of the LORD, and verse 19 states the purpose of the whole: so that your trust may be in the LORD.
historical:
The Words of the Wise have a famous parallel. In the 1920s scholars published an Egyptian wisdom text, the Instruction of Amenemope, preserved mainly on a papyrus in the British Museum. Written by an Egyptian official for his son, it is divided into thirty chapters, and its sayings closely resemble parts of Proverbs 22:17 to 23:11: inclining the ear to hear, not robbing the poor or crushing the afflicted, avoiding the hot-tempered man, not moving the ancient boundary marker, and a closing picture of a skilled scribe who is fit to stand before kings. Its date is debated, but it is usually placed somewhere around the late second millennium or early first millennium BC.

Most scholars conclude that the Israelite collector knew Amenemope's work, directly or through intermediaries, and adapted it, reshaping its advice around trust in the LORD (verse 19) and the LORD's defense of the poor (verse 23). A minority have argued that the influence ran the other way or that both drew on a common tradition. Either way, the parallel shows that Israel's sages engaged the wisdom of neighboring cultures and brought it under the rule of Israel's God.
cultural:
Verse 7 states a hard social fact: the borrower is slave to the lender. In ancient Israel a person unable to repay a debt could be forced into servitude, and creditors could take children as payment (2 Kings 4:1; Nehemiah 5:1-5). The law limited such servitude and required release in the seventh year (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12), but the danger was real. Verses 26 and 27 follow from it: a man who pledged security for another's debt and could not pay might lose even the bed he slept on.

Verse 28 forbids moving an ancient boundary stone. Family land was marked by stones set up generations earlier, and moving one at night could quietly transfer part of a field from a weak family to a strong one. The law cursed anyone who did it (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17), and the saying recurs in 23:10, where it is specifically the fields of the fatherless that are threatened. Verse 22 mentions crushing the afflicted at the gate, where the town's court met; the poor, with no one to speak for them, were easily wronged there. Verse 13's lazy man who claims there is a lion in the street is a comic figure, inventing dangers to avoid work.
literary: The chapter falls into two parts. Verses 1 to 16 continue the Solomonic collection's two-line sayings, with a concentration on wealth and poverty: the rich and poor share a Maker (verse 2), the rich rule the poor (verse 7), the generous share bread with the poor (verse 9), and oppressing the poor leads to want (verse 16). Verses 17 to 21 form a formal introduction to a new collection, with a call to listen, a statement of purpose, and a promise of thirty sayings. From verse 22 on, most sayings are commands with a reason (for, or, if), a pattern that continues into chapter 23. Verse 20's thirty is a textual puzzle: the Hebrew consonants have been read as formerly, as excellent things, or, in light of Amenemope's thirty chapters, as thirty, which most modern translations adopt.

outline.t: A good name, one Maker, humility, and the prudent
Training a child, debt, injustice, and generosity
Mockers, pure hearts, the slacker's lion, and the poor
The words of the wise: a call to listen and trust the LORD
Defending the poor, avoiding the angry, debts, boundaries, and skill

doctrines.note: The rich and the poor have this in common: the LORD is Maker of them all (verse 2). Social rank does not reach down to what people most deeply are, creatures of one God.

The LORD will take up the case of the poor and plunder those who rob them (verse 23). He is the advocate of those who have no one else to plead for them in court, and oppression of the poor is a case brought against God himself.

Verse 6 urges parents to train a child in the way he should go, and verse 15 speaks of discipline that drives folly away. Child-rearing is a serious task with long consequences, though the book does not promise that every child will turn out well.

The Words of the Wise state their purpose plainly: so that your trust may be in the LORD (verse 19). Wisdom gathered even from other peoples' teachers is meant to lead the reader to trust in Israel's God.

words.note: Chanakh, to train or dedicate. The verb is rare. Elsewhere it means to dedicate a new house (Deuteronomy 20:5) or the temple (1 Kings 8:63), and the related noun names the dedication of the altar; the later Jewish festival Hanukkah takes its name from the same root. In verse 6 it suggests both starting a child off and dedicating him to a path. Whether that path is the moral way he should go or the way suited to his own nature and stage of life is debated.

Shalish, a word related to three, used of officers or high-ranking men and here in the textual puzzle of verse 20. The written Hebrew can be read as formerly, and a traditional marginal reading gives excellent things or noble sayings. Many modern translations, including the BSB, read thirty, noting the thirty chapters of Amenemope. The uncertainty affects only the heading, not the sayings that follow.

Gevul, boundary or border, and by extension the territory it marks. The ancient boundary of verse 28 was a stone set up to mark a family's inherited land. Because the land was held as a gift from the LORD (Leviticus 25:23), moving the marker was more than theft; it undid an inheritance.

christ: Verse 2's claim that the LORD made both rich and poor stands behind the New Testament's refusal to honor the rich above the poor in the church (James 2:1-7). Verse 9's generous man who shares his bread has a later echo. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) adds a line after verse 8 saying that God blesses a cheerful giver, and Paul's words that God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7) appear to draw on it. The Words of the Wise also show a pattern the New Testament follows: taking what is true in other traditions and placing it under the true God, as Paul did when he quoted Greek poets in Athens to point to the God who raised Jesus (Acts 17:28-31). And the teacher who calls the reader to listen so that his trust may be in the LORD (verse 19) anticipates the one in whom, Paul says, are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). These are connections of theme and practice, not predictions.

hard.q: Verse 6 says a well-trained child will not depart from the way. What about faithful parents whose children walk away?
hard.a:
This verse has brought comfort to many parents and deep pain to others, especially when it is read as a promise that good parenting guarantees a faithful child. That reading misunderstands what a proverb is. Like the rest of the collection, verse 6 describes how life usually goes: early training tends to shape a whole life. It is a true and encouraging generalization, not a contract. Proverbs itself shows that children make their own choices, repeatedly warning sons who have been taught well not to abandon their teaching (for example 19:27), and Scripture tells of good parents with wayward children and bad parents with faithful ones. Ezekiel 18 insists that each generation answers for its own choices.

Interpreters also differ on what the way he should go means. Many read it as the moral and spiritual way of wisdom. Others read it as training suited to the child's own character or stage of life. A few read the verse as ironic: let a child go his own way and he will never leave it, which would make it a warning rather than a promise. On any reading, the verse urges parents to take their task seriously; it does not make them the sole cause of their children's faith or unbelief, and it does not permit anyone to blame grieving parents for a child's choices.

questions: Verse 1 says a good name is more desirable than great riches. What would you be willing to give up to keep your integrity intact?
Verse 2 says the rich and poor share one Maker. How would your church or workplace look different if that truth shaped who gets honored?
The Words of the Wise borrowed from Egyptian wisdom and placed it under the LORD. What wisdom from outside the church have you found true, and how do you bring it under Scripture?
